title: The Plume
text:
If only the sun would shine tonight

If, in the depths of the Opera, two clear and radiant breasts

Composed for the word love the most marvelous living illuminated initial

If the wooden pavement opened over the summit of the mountains

If the ermine looked with a beseeching gesture

At the red-bandaged priest

Who returns from prison counting the closed cars

If the luxurious echo of the rivers I torment

Would only cast my body onto the grass of Paris

That does not freeze inside the jewelry shops

At least spring would no longer frighten me

If only I were a root of the tree of heaven

At last goodness in the sugarcane of air

What do you see, beautiful silent one

Beneath the Arc de Triomphe of the Carrousel

If pleasure ruled under the aspect of an eternal passerby

While the Chambers were furrowed only by the violet gaze of the promenades

What would I not give for an arm of the Seine to slide beneath the Morning

Which is lost in any case

I do not resign myself, no, to the caressing rooms

Where the telephone of the night's fines rings

On leaving I set fire to a lock of hair

which is the fuse of a bomb

And the lock of hair digs a tunnel beneath Paris

If only my train would enter through that tunnel
editorial_note: The translation preserves Breton’s conditional cascade, Parisian locations, and explosive hair-fuse image.

title: The Sexual Eagle Exults Once More...
text:
The sexual eagle exults once more, it will gild the earth

Its descending wing

Its ascending wing imperceptibly stirs the stems of

hot mint

And the adorable undressing of water

The days are counted so clearly

That the mirror has made room for a latticework of foliage

I see no more of the sky than a star

Around us there is only milk describing its

vertiginous ellipse

From which the soft intuition of dark-circled agate eyelids

sometimes rises to drive the tip of its parasol into

the mud of electric light

Then expanses cast anchor, unfold along

the depths of my closed gaze

Icebergs radiating the habits of worlds to come

Born from a particle of you, from an unknown

and frozen particle that takes flight

Your existence is the giant bouquet escaping my arms

Badly tied, it opens walls, unfurls the stairways of houses

It sheds its petals in the shop windows of streets

With the news I keep leaving, with the news

The newspaper is now made of glass, and if the letters no longer arrive

it is because the train has been eaten

The great incision in the emerald that gave rise to the foliage

is scarred forever, the snow sawmills

dazzling

And the quarries of flesh hum alone at the first flash

Inverted in this flash

I acquire the imprint of life and death

In liquid air
editorial_note: The translation preserves the surreal body, liquid-air, and life-and-death imagery; the source’s broken line continuations remain line-for-line.

title: World in a Kiss
text:
World in a kiss

The musician with hazel drumsticks sewn into his sleeves

Calms a swarm of young monkey-lions

that came down with great clamor from the cornice

Everything grows opaque; I see the carriage of night pass

Dragged by axolotls in blue shoes

that enters, radiant, through the violence leading to the tomb

paved with eyelids and their eyelashes

The law of retaliation employs a people of stars

And you take on for me the hues of a black dew

While the horrible mental terminals

split open along their length

making way for plumes

that gaze at the nearby lake

The bars of the spectacle are marvelously twisted

A long spindle of air bears witness only to man's flight

At daybreak among the illustrious alfalfa

The hour

is only what the gold pieces of Bohemia make ring

on the blades of coriaria

An amazon standing on a tawny-gray horse at a gallop

From far away the arms are always in lateral extension

The dusty diamond of the lining reminds me

of the shop decorated with blue bison

by the Indians of the pillow

Outside, the air tries on mistletoe gloves

on a counter of pure water

World in a clean kiss

For me, the scales

The scales of the great celestial tortoise with a hydrofilic belly

that struggles each night in love

with the great black tortoise, the gigantic scolopendra of roots
editorial_note: The translation retains the deliberately impossible animals, objects, and celestial tortoise imagery without explaining the surreal transitions.

title: Sunflower
text:
The traveler who crossed Les Halles as summer fell

walked on tiptoe

Despair made its great yarrow plants whirl in the sky, so beautiful

And in the handbag lay my dream, that vial of salts

which only God's godmother inhaled

The torpors unfolded like vapor

in the Smoking Dog

where pro and con had just entered

The girl could be seen by them only poorly and askance

I had to deal with the ambassador of saltpeter

or with the white curve on a black background we call thought

The dance of the innocents was at its height

The little lanterns slowly lit among the chestnut trees

The lady without a shadow knelt on the Pont au Change

On Gît-le-Coeur Street the bells were no longer the same

The promises of the nights were finally being fulfilled

The carrier pigeons, the kisses of rescue

joined themselves to the breasts of the beautiful unknown

thrown beneath the crêpe of perfect meanings

A farm flourished in the middle of Paris

and its windows looked out over the Milky Way

But no one inhabited it yet because of the apparitions

of the apparitions who, as everyone knows, are more devout

than the disappeared

Some, like this woman, seem to swim

and a little of their substance enters love

She internalizes them

I am no toy of any sensory power

And yet the cricket that sang in the ash-colored hair

one afternoon near the statue of Étienne Marcel

winked at me in understanding

André Breton told me, come in
editorial_note: Les Halles, Pont au Change, Gît-le-Coeur, and Étienne Marcel are retained as Parisian referents; “yaros” is rendered as yarrow.

title: Hotel of Sparks
text:
The philosophical butterfly

settles on the pink star

and thus forms a window of hell

The masked man is always standing before the naked woman

whose hair slips just as, in the morning, the light of a lamp

that they forgot to extinguish

The wise furniture prepares the room that performs sleight of hand

with its rosettes

its circular rays of sunlight

its glass grindings

inside which a sky blues with precision

in memory of the inimitable breast

Now the cloud of a garden passes over the head of the man

who has just sat down

It splits in half the woman with the magical bust and Parma eyes

It is the hour when the boreal bear, with an expression of great intelligence

stretches and accounts for a day

On the other side, rain rears over the boulevards of a great city

Rain through the fog with rivulets of sunlight over red flowers

Rain and the diabolo of olden times

Legs beneath the fruit-bearing cloud surround the greenhouse

Only the pulse of a very white hand is perceived, represented

by two tiny wings

The seesaw of absence swings between the four walls

Splitting heads

From which flocks of kings escape and immediately wage war

Until the eastern eclipse

Turquoise at the bottom of the cups

reveals the equilateral bed of sheets the color of those flowers called

snowballs

The delightful bedside tables, the torn curtains

within reach of a little book bearing these words stamped on it

There is no tomorrow

whose author bears a strange name

in the dark terrestrial signage
editorial_note: The translation preserves the dream logic of the masked man, magical woman, eastern eclipse, and “There is no tomorrow.”

title: The Writings Fly
text:
The satin of pages leafed through in books models

a woman so beautiful

that when one is not reading, one looks at that woman sadly

without daring to speak to her, without daring to tell her she is so beautiful

that what one is about to learn is priceless

This woman passes imperceptibly amid a murmur of flowers

Sometimes she turns among the printed seasons

to ask the time, or better still pretends to contemplate some

jewels straight on

as real creatures do not

And the world dies, a rupture occurs in the rings of air

A tear in the place of the heart

The morning papers bring singers whose voices have the color of

sand on tender and dangerous riverbanks

And sometimes the evening papers give way to girls leading

chained animals

But the most beautiful thing lies in the interval between certain letters

where hands whiter than the horn of the stars at noon

plunder a nest of white swallows

so that it may always rain

so low, so low that the wings can no longer mingle

Hands by which one climbs to arms so light

that the vapor of meadows in their graceful spirals above

the ponds is their imperfect mirror

Arms that articulate only with the exceptional danger of a

body made for love

whose belly calls to the sighs shed by the thickets

full of veils

and that have of the earthly only the immense frozen truth of the sleds of

gazes across the whole white expanse

of what I will never see again

because of a marvelous blindfold

which is mine in the game of blindman's buff played with wounds
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s book-and-body metamorphosis and its final blindfold image.

title: Yves Tanguy’s House
text:
The house of Yves Tanguy

where one enters only at night


With the storm-lamp


Outside, the transparent country

A diviner in his element


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen


And the printed fabric of the sky

—Bring the supernatural down to earth


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen

With all the stars of hell


Made of loops and jambs

Crab-colored in the surf


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen

With all the stars of hell

With the delirious streetcars held back only by their cables


Space chained, time diminished

Ariana in her little chest-room


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen

With all the stars of hell

With the delirious streetcars held back only by their cables

With the argonaut's endless manes


The service is run by moths

who cover their eyes with cloth


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen

With all the stars of hell

With the delirious streetcars held back only by their cables

With the argonaut's endless manes

With the desert's blazing furniture


There one kills, there one heals

And conspires without concealment


With the storm-lamp

With the sawmill so industrious that it can no longer be seen

With all the stars of hell

With the delirious streetcars held back only by their cables

With the argonaut's endless manes

With the desert's blazing furniture

With the signals lovers exchange from afar


That is the house of Yves Tanguy.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the cumulative refrain and the surreal house inventory; “lámpara-tempestad” is rendered as “storm-lamp.”

title: To the Ship
text:
Ode imitated from Horace's O Navis, Referent.


What new hopes

carry you to the sea? Turn back,

turn back, audacious ship,

to your native shore.


You still see a thousand memories

of the past storm,

and already you fling yourself

a second time into fortune?


Your course is strewn with

stealthy shoals,

where too late the sounding line

will warn of dangers.


Ah! Turn back, there is still time,

while the sea caresses the shells

of the shore

with peaceful waves.


Soon, bristling into hills,

it will come battering the rocks,

and shipwrecked

relics make a carpet for Neptune.


The pretentious pomp

of silk streamers

does not fear the insults

of sonorous tempest.


What are bars and lions

against the Euro,

tyrant of the waves,

on your gilded stern?


What is your name, famous

in kingdoms of the dawn,

and where, for the sun,

its crystal chamber receives it?


Yesterday on these waters,

confident in itself,

another arrogant prow

challenged the wind;


and now, an ill-fated monument

that astonishes the sailor,

on a naked reef

it lies covered with algae.


What! Do you not hear me? Do you not alter

your course? Proudly choose

new sails,

and without fear put out to sea?


Do you not see, poor wretch,

that the sky is already clouding,

and the clouds, bellowing,

give birth to lightning?


Do you not see the hoary foam,

swollen into turmoil,

nor does the gale frighten you,

whistling in the rigging?


Turn back, beloved object

of my anxious concern;

turn back to the friendly shore,

before the sun goes down!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Horatian ship ode, maritime warnings, and repeated appeals to turn back. This record is the valid ship-poem body; the neighboring “A Moisés” record is excluded for title mismatch.

title: The Anauco
text:
Let greed urge
along unknown routes
toward sonorous Tethys
and roaring south winds
the pine that inhabited
the pleasant banks
of fortunate Baetis,
dressed in amaranth;
let it safely admire
the delicious fields
of the mighty Ganges,
crowned with fragrances.


You, green and peaceful
bank of the Anauco,
for me more joyful
than the Idalian woods
and the beautiful meadows
of tranquil Paphos,
you will resound continually
with my humble songs;
and when my shadow
upon the fatal boat
visits the solitary valleys
of Erebus,
in your shaded forests
and secluded caves
I shall wander as one day,
perhaps abandoning
the silent bank
of the Stygian lakes.


The sorrowing crowd
of the nearby villages
will summon my manes
with mournful weeping;
and before the sad tomb,
dressed in funeral branches
and fragrant
with Indian perfumes,
Phyllis will say, weeping:
“Here Fabio rests.”


A thousand times fortunate!
But you, unhappy one,
through barbarous nations,
far from your native climate,
may you falter weakly
under the weight of years.
May the bloodthirsty dogs
that Charybdis feeds
on her rough crags
devour your corpse;
nor may the treacherous wife,
girded by other arms,
soothe your ashes
with grief-stricken cries.
editorial_note: Classical names and allusions—Tethys, Baetis, Ganges, Paphos, Erebus, and Charybdis—are retained.

title: How Many Stars Are in the Sky?
text:
“The last night we spent together,

asked:

—How many stars are there in the sky?

—Three hundred and fifty thousand.

—Bet you can't.

—Bet I can.


—Be quiet. Tonight

I do not want you asking such things.

Tonight, if you want to ask

how many stars there are in the sky,

or anything else,

ask something like: Do you love me?

Are you cold? Who says they are hungry?


Tonight, ask something that can be

answered in the wordless world.

Question with all your blood

something in which all the world's life

is asking,

something like: Who is crying?

Is anything needed?


And you will see how everything is needed,

and you will know how many stars there are in the sky

when you know that the sky has a single star

for each moment,

because if one is lost,

the light of the Universe will take one step into shadow.”
editorial_note: The source begins with a stray closing quotation mark and ends with an opening one; the English repairs the enclosing punctuation while documenting the source anomaly.

title: La Parima and the Springs
text:
La Parima is the pharaonic dream

and Moses' stone,

the Sister's black honeycomb,

which Brother Francis did not come to know.

Cathedral of mystery, Southern Range, unknown,

hidden tongue of the voice of water,

God's badly closed eyelid, letting show

the blue thread of a glance.


I dreamed, for your Glory,

river of the Homeland,

of writing an essential word

on the sheet of the savanna,

wetting in your dark springs

the celestial sting of a heron's feather.

But I found only my blood,

its red thinned by the mixture of tears.


Yet I offered to come to you

and I am on your path!

You will emerge from your springs: the God of Parima,

the Indian God, will open the door for you

of his great dark house; the Old God

will let you come as he does every day,

and I will be on your path…

You emerge from the hands of your mountain,

as a miracle emerges from the hand of God,

as every night, from the cage of the sky,

the Bird of the Sun escapes and goes to the fields.
editorial_note: La Parima, the Southern Range, and the Indigenous/Old God imagery are retained; “Sister” and “Brother Francis” follow the source’s capitalized kinship terms.

title: The Orbit of Water
text:
Come, friends, let us embark

on the journey of the drop of water.

It is a drop, barely, like a bird's eye.


For us it is only a point,

a seed of light,

a seed of water,

half the tears of a smile,

but the sky fits inside it

and it would be the shipwreck of an ant.


Come, friends, let us follow

the orbit of the drop of water:

From the crest of a wave

it leaps, with the morning vapor;

it rises to the shore of a cloud

islanded in the sky, white as a beach;

it travels toward the West,

rains on a mountain peak,

brightens the leaves,

glazes the shoots,

rolls through a ravine,

is seasoned in the juice of fallen fruit,

jumps in the waterfalls,

flows into the river, runs toward the East,

cuts the savanna in two,

performs pirouettes in the whirlpools,

and in the broad still pools expands

like a cat's pupil,

continues eastward on the ebb tide,

reaches the sea, the crest of its wave,

and we have arrived, friends… We will return tomorrow.
editorial_note: The translation follows the drop’s complete orbit and preserves the recurring address to the friends.

title: Chorus of the Provinces
text:
Violent with harmony, in the tone of the undertow,

the chorus of the seven provinces arrives,

seven adolescent faces

at the seven windows

of the stars of Autonomy.

They sing. The childhood of the Homeland sings with them,

dripping the first milk from its lips;

the first blond light descends from the stars,

sewing the button of the ear into the cornfields;

the chorus of the provinces dances,

in the republican classroom.

But they dance upon the grass

blue with fantasy,

upon Miranda's sky

pierced by masts while the squadron sails.


The Guayanese word

is not in the chorus of the seven nymphs,

and in them they reverse the course of the sky

and sail eastward like the Seven Sisters;

and there they see the miracle of the Earth:

on one side, virgin gold lays down a yellow strip,

toward the North, on the other side,

the Eastern Pampas, red with Reconquest,

and in the middle a blue river,

and there they see themselves reflected and nest in its center.

And so the river became its strip of sky

that presides over the dance of the seven provinces.
editorial_note: The translation retains Venezuelan referents including Miranda, Guayana, the Eastern Pampas, and the Seven Sisters.

title: Invocation to the God of Waters
text:
Submarine God, lake God, river God,

one in the triton and the heron

and in the gentle corvette and the rough cruiser,

God of water, Lord of the Crystal House,

Sailor God.

Expression of water in your thousand expressions,

river stretched from Volturno to Christ,

flight of the ibis that crosses

from the figurehead of the Argo

to the mast of the Santa Maria, Argonaut God,

who extends to the hands of Harmony

the river of your music, long as a flute.

God infused in the white lake of the cloud

bordered in blue,

God of foam in the lamb's curl,

storm God in the lion's mane,

God the diviner, stilled in the tiger's pupil,

God of the river of stars that from East to West

crosses the sky at night,

God of the combatant water

in the maned Niagara and the suspicious Dardanelles:


Extend your right hand where the River is born

and your left where it empties

—in a crystal arch of Brahma—

extend the amphora of your hands,

Lord of Water, Old Commander,

toward the sonorous springs,

toward the warm still pool

of the belligerent-water Orinoco,

sprung from your temples, sweated from your pores

on the Saturday of your first rest!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the long invocation’s catalog of water forms, mythic vessels, rivers, and the final Orinoco image.

title: She Died Again One Day...
text:
One day she died again… I loved her,

but without remedy she died that day…

—Come back, Rabbi, come back!… I cried—

but the blond Rabbi did not return.


The girl passed twenty centuries dead,

Palestine's Capernaum died,

and my soul, useless and desolate,

wept immortally over the ruins.


And I loved her, loved her… Her whiteness

I sought in the white nebula,

her hair amid the dark night

and her rose color in the West…


And at last I found her… Hidden among the tulle

of a sunset, there she was;

her motionless flesh between two blues

inaugurated the first star…


And I found her whiter still,

floating in the blue, unclothed,

how white she was like that!… my girl

had twenty centuries of whiteness…


I cried to Love then… Good voices

said from far away: “He has heard you!”

I cried to eternal Love… and at my side

the white girl was scarcely a cloud…


Love came. The heavens fell silent,

his light step silenced the sphere,

eternal love came barefoot,

the hair of his head ripened wheat…


“She is not dead… She sleeps!” And he commanded her:

—Rise!

and she rose, slender with martyrdom,

and a voice climbed her throat

like a bee leaving a lily.


And she has returned to me… her dark hair,

her same voice… but in her cold hand,

with twenty centuries of kneading whiteness,

the fear of dying one day persists….
editorial_note: The translation preserves the resurrection-like return, the repeated whiteness, and the source’s ellipses and abrupt commands.

title: The Future Boat
text:
River of the Seven Stars,

path of the Liberator,

blood of the Heart of America,

aorta that does not leave the heart!


Thin river of the springs,

angry river of the falls,

river of the seven stars,

that at the Source do not fill the hollow of the hands

and then become the dream of a sea without restraint!


Bewitching river, that paints yourself with every sky,

River of La Urbana, pampas plain,

River of San Félix, solution of glory,

River of Angostura, channel of war,

River of Barrancas, River of thinking

how there can be so much water on Earth,

River of our Hope,

when Hope shall be!

River of us, our very mirror,

mirror of this soul of ours,

through which, tireless as you are for horizons,

we sweat through twists and turns!

I shall not lay my hands upon your back,

I shall not paint your banks,

for if on the left you have the heart of the cities,

on the right you raise the arm of the forests;

I shall not touch your waters, your millions of drops,

which are the tithe of the peaks for the worship of the prairies,

I shall not walk upon your waves,

for the Master will come walking upon them.


I only want to widen my eyes

toward the future procession sailing upon your waters

and toward the procession of the past,

toward reality and promise,

toward Antonio Díaz's boat

and toward the deep dream in which you dream

of the prow of the battleship,

as peasant children dream of their string steamboat,

of the steel ship

that will advance toward your springs haloed with sails,

and with the rainbow's dove standing at the masthead,

its breast opened by your Seven Stars…
editorial_note: The source contains a stray “P>” marker before “No he de poner”; it is removed from the English and the paragraph break it interrupted is restored, documented here as an OCR artifact.

title: The Sweet Sickness
text:
I turn my eyes toward my own history.

Dreams, more dreams and more dreams… glory,

more glory… hatred… a nightingale fleeing…

and I am astonished not to see in all of it

a feature, a sketch, or a trace

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


I turn again to look along the road traveled…

My march was a soldier's march,

with a victorious step, amid all the din;

my joy a barbarous joy…

And nowhere yet is there the shadow

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


A summit rose before me; a thousand others tried

to crown it and could not;

only I remained above, smiling,

and there, with my voice released, my arm outstretched,

I never felt even the slightest peck

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


I turned my brow toward the most beautiful sunset…

a thousand brave men yielded to defeat,

but I was victor over the terrible evil;

I was purple, evening glory,

without sensing the clandestine march

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


Forces and powers besieged me

and, trial upon trial, hemmed in

my faith, which I neither exchange nor sell,

and I watched them march away in spite

of their spite, happy, without sensing anything in my breast

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


Women… for my glory and my struggles

many were given to me in many places,

and everywhere I fell asleep loving,

and in the morning I went on toward another love,

but in none did I sense the dart

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


And one day came the awkward circumstance

of our being alone in the room,

reading together without reading,

looking into each other's eyes without malice,

and afterward remaining with the delight

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated refrain and the movement from public glory to private recognition of the “sweet sickness.”

title: Angostura
text:
In Angostura, the river

becomes thin and deep like a secret,

it has the intensity of an idea

that puts the wrinkle on the Middle Rock.


In Angostura, the water

has the depth of a concept,

and perhaps here the river is Bolívar's shadow,

metaphor for a soul that cannot fit inside the body.


See how it comes downstream;

think something in the river without fences or ports,

broad as far as the horizon,

hot as the Desert.

The boat is an instant in the life of water,

a leaf on a tree, a note in thunder,

and in the boat came the hope of America,

a mere sip of a man, a feather in flight,

the first drop where there is born

the Orinoco of Dream.

And it arrived here, at Angostura, on a primitive beach;

the canoe moored; see him sink into the ground

the fine heel, with the sting

of the wasp that wants to know its hive;

follow him, climbing the slope

toward the city; a flutter

of bells announces his arrival, the houses

don their Sunday clothes of flags and signs,

from Soledad canoes arrive with women

like baskets of mangoes and mereyes in season.

Angostura struts its jaunty elegance

to please the handsome Hero with black eyes.


And when he climbed the stairway

toward the summit of the Congress,

and when he turned back toward the beach

with the Republic in his chest,

what was that light, Orinoco,

that ruffled your muscles and bristled your nerves

and shook your deep fibers

from the foot of Maipures to the fist of Macareo?

Was it not the Homeland? Was it not the Homeland itself?

The age-old homeland born in your womb

and destined to live through the centuries, eternal as the World,

because if one day it dies within us, you will return from the Ocean.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Angostura, Bolívar, Maipures, Macareo, and the river-as-Homeland metaphor.

title: Indigenous Evocation
text:
Going up toward San Félix, where the river shows two teeth,

where the river shows, tightly clenched,

the two fists of Piar squeezing the Deed,

going up toward San Félix, we saw the rainbow

that made the Indian bow on its string of waters.

And then I remembered, friends,

that lesson in History we read in childhood,

the first lesson in History,

in which our legend inaugurates the soul:

Remember the first lesson:

it tells us that Columbus discovered us on his third voyage

and speaks of those currents that stopped Columbus.


A simple History class, clear as a morning,

simple as the day of the first sweetheart,

the dream of first dawns,

a simple History class, like a Sunday,

with eight o'clock Mass and starched clothes,

a History class that tells us of the day

when the caravels from Spain were coming,

while, indifferent to everything that might come from the sea,

Sorocaima searched the mountains for flowers for his beloved.

Through the stormy strait,

the three caravels advance,

another sail is raised in the foam

that fans the stones of the coast of Paria,

the three caravels come,

but on the Indians' side the twenty mouths await them.


And as they head toward the free Ocean,

a shadow rises;

its legs spread across the Delta,

clinging to the soil that keeps its treasures,

the Orinoco of its wet thighs,

with gold in its feet and the Sun on its back

and its head among the heavens,

in one hand it holds a bow and shoots twenty arrows,

and the three ships struggle to advance in vain

because at the Delta they are repelled by

the old autonomous Indian,

who was born in Parima and grew up in Guayana,

and draws the indigenous bow—yes, draws the rainbow bow—

and shoots twenty arrows as twenty herons fly…
editorial_note: The translation retains the historical names and the final transformation of the Indigenous bow into a rainbow bow.
